newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Europe car makers seek niches in saturated market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Europe car makers seek niches in saturated market.

text.p: Europe's car makers, facing saturated markets and dismal prospects for growth, are hoping that novel new products will transform their fortunes.
New minicars and mini multi-purpose vehicles (MPVs) will be taking centre stage at the Paris Car Show which opens on Thursday (Oct 3).
The little Ford Ka is the first in a new wave of minicars destined for Europe.
Renault's Megane Scenic, a smaller version of the highly successful Espace MPV, was shown to the public at Geneva earlier this year, and is now almost ready for the customer.
Most of the big six car manufacturers are thought to be planning similar vehicles to the Scenic and the Ka, but for the moment Renault and Ford are alone.

MPVs, like the Espace and Chrysler Caravan, known as Minivans in the United States, can seat up to eight. They resemble vans with windows, but cosset the occupants in relative luxury. They are expensive and guzzle fuel.
Lighter, more economic and cheaper mini MPVs seat up to five, and offer families more versatility in stowing bikes, luggage and tents.

"There are two important novelties at Paris; the Ford Ka and the Scenic. Both are indicative of the way manufacturers are thinking about future segmentation of the European market," said John Lawson, European automotive analyst at Salomon Brothers.
"They are both first into the niche products, in what ought to be a very vibrant and growing segment in Europe in the next five years," Lawson said.
And the big six car makers in Europe -- Germany's Volkswagen AG, Italy's Fiat, Ford and General Motors of the United States and France's Renault and Peugeot -- could do with a boost.
Sales dived by more than two million in 1993, when recession shaken western European car markets skidded by 15 percent, the steepest annual decline in 50 years.

Since then sales have stumbled along, often boosted by incentive schemes to replace older, polluting cars. Car companies have been forced to fight for every sale, offering incentives and deep price cuts.
If they didn't have enough problems, along came the need for governments to deflate economies to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria for European monetary union.

Arthur Maher, automotive analyst at McGraw Hill's DRI, says sales growth this year in Europe, expected to be between five and six percent at about 12.6 million, is really only two percent when subsidies and incentives are accounted for.
"On the surface five to six percent looks good, but underlying sentiment is quite different because sales have been artificially stimulated by incentives," Maher said.

"Two thirds of the growth seen cannot be attributed to consumers. One third of the increase this year is down to government incentives, and another third to manufacturers' incentives. If left to real spending power we'd be looking at two percent growth this year not six percent," Maher said.
Prospects for the rest of the century will not fill shareholders with glee.
According to a report by the Economist Intelligence Unit, sales will rise slowly to a peak of about 12.55 million in 1998, and then gradually fall away again to around 12.3 million in 2000.
And if that's not enough to phase shareholders try this.

"European governments will actively discourage car usage, with high traffic density and significant pollution problems leading to rationing of road space by road tolls, and more taxes on fuel and engine size. A carbon tax will almost certainly be imposed within the next few years," the EIU report said.

"Car production capacity is predicted to increase by 16 percent by 2000, yet demand will increase by just over two percent. Manufacturers...will also be forced increasingly into cutting prices or offering higher specifications for the same price," the report said.
Peter Schmidt, analyst with Automotive Industry Data, says the industry has scaled back over-optimistic forecasts and buckled down to the new circumstances.
"We used to be told that sales would reach 15, maybe 17 million a year; we would all have two or three cars. Now it is accepted that the market is saturated," says Schmidt.
Schmidt reckons that manufacturers have identified narrow growth sectors -- like the retired and women -- and are designing products like the little Ka which appeal to them.
"This is the recipe for future survival. Preparing yourself with all these niche sector products; taking precautions for the saturated market ahead and thinning margins," Schmidt said.

Salomon Brothers' Lawson says that because of likely restrictions on car use, and higher road and fuel taxes, the future of the industry is with small cars. Even manufacturers like Mercedes are diving in.
"In five years time mini city cars will be mainstream for the industry, no longer in peripheral vision," Lawson says.
At the Paris Mondial de l'Automobile, new models will be thin on the ground, after a surge of new cars last year.

VW will show its new Passat large family saloon. Japan's Nissan Motor Co Ltd takes the dust covers off its Primera, while Ford will unveil its revamped Mondeo, both large family cars. Renault will show its new Espace.
Dreamers can ogle new sportscars like the Porsche Boxster and the Jaguar XK8. The Jaguar, unveiled at Geneva, will shortly go on sale across the world.
